doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Meeting Adrian Rollini at the Hotel New Yorker with a bass sax pad
summary: At 16 Davern brought Adrian Rollini a bass saxophone pad; Rollini was moved, and Davern later learned he was murdered.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Tony DeNicola is my favorite drummer because he really takes me home, and Greg Cohn is just a very intuitive, deeply rooted musician who’s heard and cares. Well the story I’ll tell you about, speaking of caring, I once drove to, when I was 16 years old, I drove to the Hotel New Yorker at 10:30 at night, parked my car on the street, which you could do then, painted in my moustache and drew up my double breasted suit and shirt and tie and I’m walking in the door and this goon who is standing at the door says, “Yeah kid?” I said, “Oh I want to see Mr. Rollini.” Adrian Rollini, who was playing vibes with this trio at Adrian’s Tap Room, which at that time was at the Hotel New Yorker on the corner of 34th and Eighth, the entrance was right there. I had acquired that very day two bass saxophone pads from his original bass saxophone that was in the shop where I used to go to get my horn worked on, on 48th Street. And when I looked over, it was Freddie Davis’ repair shop, and I saw this great big beautiful silver ba— a Conn bass saxophone sitting on the mantle. I said to Freddie, I said, “Whose is that?” He said, “Adrian Rollini’s.” “No kidding? What are you going to do with the pads?” He says, “Well I’m going to throw them away.” I said, “Well can I have the B flat and the E flat?” He says, “Why sure” he says. And later, “Freddie, I’ll take the middle G.” And I knew that the middle G was played all the time, but the low B flat not all the time you see? So I was thinking about, I had just come on to Bix Beiderbecke with Rollini, the bass saxophone playing, which I thought was nonparalleled, just the greatest thing I ever heard. So now I’m walking into

this place and this goon is, “What do you want kid.” I said, “I want to see Mr. Rollini.” He looked at his watch and said, “Sit over there at that table, kid.” I said okay. I thought I could pass but obviously I failed. So anyway I’m sitting at the table and Rollini is just finishing up, six people in the joint. Six people. Rollini gets off the stand and he’s walking sort of dejectedly toward the door. I said, “Mr. Rollini?” He says, “Yeah.” I reach in my pocket and I said, “You know what these are?” And I handed him the bass saxophone pad. And he looked up and he says, “Where’d you get these?” And I said, “From Freddie Davis’.” He says, “Well what are you doing with them?” I said, “Well,” I said, “I really love what you played when you played with Bix Beiderbecke, I thought your playing was just superb. ‘Goose Pimples’ and ‘Jazz Band Ball.’” And he grabbed hold of the chair and tears came to his eyes and he said, “I didn’t think anybody cared anymore.” And he signed it to me, to Kenny, sincerely, Adrian, and the date. I’ve got that pad in there. Yeah. Had the original shellac on the back and the whole thing. Yeah. But there, you see? He had given up you know. He was just really sour about everything. And I found out a few years later, murdered. It was a mob rubout.

Yeah he was a heavy inveterate gambler. And he was into them for a lot of money and I guess they called in their tokens. And he couldn’t do it and they found him, you know, legs broken and all that, in a ditch in one of the creeks on the east side, on the east coast of Florida.
